About: Binomial counts of independent molecules in part of a vessel

Source

Concept
The binomial distribution of the number n of independent molecules found in a counted region of a vessel, for vessels holding N = 25, 100 and 400 molecules.
Serves
Explaining how the fluctuations of the fraction n/N and of the count n depend on the number of molecules N.
Inquiry
Six question cards, each answered from the vessels, the tick rows, the inset or the measured readouts.
Misconception
Addressed inside the answer choices; each choice has its own feedback, shown once it is picked.
On screen
Main plot: the exact P(n) = N!/(n!(N − n)!)·pⁿqN−n, computed at every integer n through log-gamma, drawn as N·P(n) against n/N on fixed axes, which scales every curve to area 1. Vessels: the three vessels at the latest snapshot, every molecule at its own random position, the counted region shaded and the molecules in it coloured, with the count n and n/N above each. Tick rows: one tick per snapshot at the fraction n/N found, the latest 60 per vessel, older ones fading. Inset: P(n) against n − n̄, where n̄ = Np is the mean count. Readouts panel: the snapshot count, then the measured spread √(mean of n² − (mean of n)²) and the measured relative width (spread divided by the mean of n), each shown from the tenth snapshot on.
Controls
Counted region: left half (p = ½) or left fifth (p = ⅕), chosen with a two-option toggle; changing it clears the snapshots. Clear empties the tick rows and readouts. Play/Pause starts and stops the snapshots, taken 4 per second at 1× speed; each snapshot gives every molecule its own random position and counts those whose x is below p.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honors it
Commit before revealEvery card is a gated choice; the snapshots and the controls stay live throughout.
Staged revealsThe inset and the readout rows appear only at the cards that read them.
Operational quantitiesSpreads and relative widths are measured from the snapshots themselves, not quoted.
Stable scalesBoth plots keep the same fixed axes at both settings of the counted region.
Experiment beside theoryEach tick row shares the horizontal axis of its exact curve, so scatter and curve width compare directly.
Misconceptions handled structurallyPlausible wrong intuitions appear only as answer choices, each answered by its own feedback.
Counting Molecules in Half a Vessel
Fraction in the counted region N·P(n) against n/N · each curve scaled to area 1
Inset · probability of each count P(n) against n − n̄

Guided Inquiry

1 · Three vessels side by side

Keep the counted region at the left half and press Play. Each snapshot scatters the molecules afresh in the three vessels on the right and counts those in the shaded region; each count adds a tick at n/N beneath the main plot. After about half a minute, how does the scatter of the fraction n/N compare between the three vessels?

2 · Four times as many molecules

Press Clear and let at least 200 snapshots accumulate (about 50 s at 1×, or 13 s at 4× speed), then read the relative widths in the Readouts. By what factor does the relative width change each time the vessel holds four times as many molecules?

3 · The spread of the count

The inset has appeared below the main plot: the same three distributions drawn against the count n − n̄. The Readouts now also give the spread of the count. How does the spread of the count itself change from the vessel of 25 to the vessel of 400?

4 · Exactly half on the left

On the main plot the peak of the 400 curve is twice as tall as the peak of the 100 curve. Look at the peaks of the same two curves in the inset. What happens to the probability of finding exactly half the molecules in the left half when the vessel goes from 100 molecules to 400?

5 · Counting the left fifth

With at least 200 snapshots at the left half recorded, note the relative widths, then switch the counted region to the left fifth, p = ⅕, and let at least 200 new snapshots accumulate. The curves on the main plot move to n/N = 0.2 and become slightly narrower. What happens to the relative widths?

6 · A litre of air

Return the counted region to the left half. A litre of air at room temperature and atmospheric pressure holds about 2.5 × 10²² molecules. Following the pattern in the three relative-width readouts, what is the relative width of the number of molecules in the left half of that litre?

Counting Molecules in Half a Vessel

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Each molecule of a gas is in a chosen part of its vessel or not, independently of the others. This sim takes snapshots of three vessels, counts the molecules in the shaded region, and sets the counts beside the exact binomial distribution.

What you'll learn

  • How independent chances give the probability of finding n molecules in the counted region.
  • How the scatter of the count n and of the fraction n/N depends on the number of molecules N.
  • How the spread and the relative width σn/n̄ depend on N and on the region.
  • How the pattern carries over to the enormous N of real gas.
The set-up: three vessels, one counted region. Each snapshot scatters the molecules afresh.

What's on screen

  • Main plot: N·P(n) against n/N for N = 25 (dots), 100 (black line) and 400 (blue line), with a row of ticks beneath for each vessel: one tick per snapshot, at the n/N found.
  • Vessels (right): the latest snapshot, the counted region shaded, with n and n/N above each.
  • Inset (below the main plot): P(n) against n − n̄.
  • Readouts: snapshots taken, then the measured spread and relative width of each vessel.
See itStart taking snapshots with your current counted region. Watch for: the count n and the fraction n/N changing in every vessel at each snapshot, and ticks piling up under the plot.

Fixed: the vessels hold N = 25, 100 and 400 molecules. Every snapshot gives each molecule a new random position, and a molecule is counted when its x is below p.

03

Each molecule makes an independent draw

A molecule is in the counted region with probability p and outside it with probability q = 1 − p, whatever the others do. For the left half p = ½; for the left fifth p = ⅕. The chance of finding exactly n of the N molecules in the region is the binomial distribution of the notes:

Notes (4.1), with q = 1 − p. The binomial coefficient counts which n of the N molecules they are, and pnqN−n is the chance of any one such choice.

The probabilities add to (p + q)N = 1, and the mean count is n̄ = Np (4.2). The sim draws this for three vessels as N·P(n) against n/N, which gives every curve an area of 1.

See itCount the left half at 1× speed. Watch for: the count n in each vessel changing from one snapshot to the next, around the mean n̄ = N/2.
04

The spread of the count grows as √N

The variance of the binomial is σn2 = Npq (4.3), so the spread is

Notes (4.3). The mean grows in proportion to N; the spread grows only as √N.

At p = ½ this is √N/2: 2.5, 5 and 10 molecules for N = 25, 100 and 400. The spread doubles each time the vessel holds four times as many molecules. The inset plots P(n) against n − n̄, so the widths are in molecules: the curves get wider while their peaks fall.

The inset, left half: exact P(n) against n − n̄. The widths are the spreads σn.
See itCount the left half at 4× speed and read the measured spread. Watch for: the spread readouts settling near 2.5, 5 and 10 molecules.
05

The relative width falls as 1/√N

A measurement sees the spread compared with the mean:

Notes (4.4). The mean grows as N and the spread only as √N, so their ratio falls as 1/√N.

At p = ½, √(q/p) = 1, so the exact relative widths are 0.200, 0.100 and 0.050. The Readouts measure them from the snapshots and scatter a little around these values. Four times the molecules halves the relative width, which is why each curve on the main plot is half as wide as the one before.

A litre of air at room temperature and atmospheric pressure holds about 2.5 × 1022 molecules, so σn/n̄ = 1/√N ≈ 6 × 10−12. The count still fluctuates, by about 8 × 1010 molecules, but that is a vanishing fraction of the 1.25 × 1022 in each half.

Left half: σn/n̄ against N on logarithmic scales. The line has slope −½.
See itCount the left half at 4× speed and read the measured relative widths. Watch for: the three relative-width readouts settling near 0.20, 0.10 and 0.05.
06

An even split gets less likely as N grows

The main plot shows N·P(n), not P(n). Multiplying N by 4 doubles the peak height drawn that way, because it rises as √N (notes, Figure 25). P itself is that height divided by N, so P(N/2) is multiplied by 2/4 = ½.

The largest value of the symmetric binomial (even N), from Stirling’s approximation. It falls as 1/√N.

From N = 100 to N = 400, P(N/2) falls from 0.080 to 0.040. An even split is still the single most likely count; a bigger vessel simply has more counts near it, each with a smaller share. The inset shows these peaks directly.

See itOpen the left half with the inset in view. Watch for: the inset peaks, about 0.080 for N = 100 and 0.040 for N = 400, while the blue peak on the main plot is the tallest.
07

A smaller region widens the relative width

Switch the counted region to the left fifth: p = ⅕, q = ⅘. The mean falls to n̄ = Np = 5, 20 and 80, but the spread σn = √(Npq) falls only to 2, 4 and 8. So the relative width, √(q/p)/√N = 2/√N, doubles: 0.400, 0.200 and 0.100.

On the main plot the curves move to n/N = 0.2 and are slightly narrower, because the spread of the fraction, √(pq/N), is 0.4/√N instead of 0.5/√N. Compared with the mean they are wider: σn fell to 0.8 of its left-half value, but n̄ fell to 0.4. A smaller region holds fewer molecules to average over.

See itCount the left fifth at 4× speed and read the measured relative widths. Watch for: the three relative-width readouts settling near 0.40, 0.20 and 0.10.
08

Where it matters

  • Steady pressure and density. The pressure of a gas and the density of the air in a room do not visibly fluctuate, because each is an average over enormous numbers of molecules (notes, Section 4.1).
  • Counting rare events. When p is small, q is close to 1 and σn/n̄ is close to 1/√n̄. A detector that counts about 104 events carries a relative scatter of about 1%.
  • The random walk. N steps, each right or left with probability ½, give the same distribution (notes, Section 4.1): n steps to the right, N − n to the left.
Go deeper: where 2.5 × 1022 comes from

For an ideal gas N = pV/kBT. With the pressure of one atmosphere (101 325 Pa), V = 1 L and T = 293 K, that is about 2.5 × 1022 molecules.

09

Summary

In one line. Each molecule is in the counted region by an independent chance p, so the count n follows the binomial distribution, and the sim sets measured snapshots beside it.

Key points

  • The mean is n̄ = Np and the spread is σn = √(Npq), which grows as √N.
  • The relative width σn/n̄ = √(q/p)/√N falls as 1/√N, and is larger for a smaller region.
  • The main plot shows N·P(n); P(N/2) itself falls as 1/√N.

Common mix-ups

  • “More molecules means a wider fraction.” The spread of the count grows, from 2.5 to 10. The fraction n/N gets narrower, from 0.20 to 0.05.
  • “The relative width settles at about 0.05 once the vessel is large.” Every factor of 4 in N halves it again.
  • “The taller main-plot peak means an even split is more likely.” That plot is N·P(n). P(N/2) itself halves, from 0.080 to 0.040.

Things to try on your own

  • Press Clear, take at least 200 snapshots of the left half, and compare each measured relative width with 0.200, 0.100 and 0.050.
  • Repeat with the left fifth and note which factor the relative widths change by.
  • Take the measured spread for N = 100 and compare it with √(Npq).
